back: Bond breaking in which each atom keeps one electron, forming two free radicals (e.g. Cl₂ → 2Cl• in UV light).
Bond breaking in which one atom keeps both electrons, forming a cation and an anion.
An electron-pair donor that attacks an electron-deficient (δ+) atom, e.g. OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃, H₂O.
An electron-pair acceptor that attacks an electron-rich region, e.g. H⁺, NO₂⁺, polarised Br₂, carbocations.
A species with an unpaired electron, shown with a dot, e.g. Cl•, CH₃•.

front: What does a curly arrow show?
back: The movement of a pair of electrons, from a lone pair or bond to an atom. A fish-hook arrow shows one electron.
A small molecule (H₂O, HBr) is removed from one molecule, forming a C=C bond.
Hydrolysis splits a molecule using water; hydration adds water across a C=C bond (addition).
Tertiary > secondary > primary, because electron-donating alkyl groups disperse the positive charge.
